strengths: The paper identifies a genuine gap in discrete flow matching: the rectification/path-straightening machinery of continuous flow matching does not directly transfer, and the proposed discrete dynamic-OT objective with an equivalent Kantorovich cost (Hamming distance under the discrete metric; embedding L2 cost under Corollary 3.3) is a natural and conceptually clean analogue.

Theorem 3.1 is a useful design-space result: it shows that for convex interpolant conditional flows, the expected weighted outflow integrates exactly to the coupling cost sum_i s(x0_i, x1_i), which connects minibatch OT couplings (Tong et al. 2023; Fatras et al. 2021) to discrete flow matching in a principled way.

The perplexity bound (Theorem 4.1 / Eq. 24) addresses a real practical limitation of discrete flows—the lack of an instantaneous-change-of-variables estimator—and adapting the Opper & Sanguinetti (2007) variational approach to this setting is a reasonable strategy.
The proofs in Appendix A are largely self-contained and the derivations of Theorem 3.1 and Corollary 3.2/3.3 are straightforward to verify.
The proposed source-distribution constructions (empirical token distribution, K-means-based source) show awareness of why naive minibatch OT couplings may fail when the source is unstructured.
weaknesses: Complete absence of experiments. The paper's central claims—that the proposed objective minimizes state transitions during generation and that the perplexity bound enables performance evaluation and comparison—are never supported by any empirical evidence. There are no language-modeling results, no comparison of minibatch-OT couplings vs. independent couplings, no measurement of jump counts, and no assessment of the tightness or computability of the perplexity bound on real data. For a paper whose contributions are framed as practical improvements ('enables us to evaluate the performance of our model'), this is a fundamental evidential gap.

Limited originality. Minibatch OT couplings for flow matching are well established (Tong et al. 2023; Fatras et al. 2021), and the perplexity bound closely follows Lou et al. (2024) for discrete diffusion. The contribution is essentially a discrete-state translation of known techniques; the theory does not appear to require fundamentally new ideas beyond adapting existing machinery.

The claimed 'categorical version of the Benamou-Brenier theorem' is overstated. The equivalence in Theorem 3.1 is established only for flows induced by convex interpolant conditional velocities under a fixed coupling, not for arbitrary velocity fields. Hence the paper does not actually characterize an optimum over the dynamic formulation (no variational characterization over all flows), so minimizing the Kantorovich cost via minibatch couplings is only a heuristic, not a proven optimality statement.

The proof of Theorem 4.1 contains gaps and sloppy error control. The final step from D_KL(q0||p0) <= D_KL(path) to D_KL(q1||p1) <= D_KL(path) is justified only by a vague appeal to 'reverse processes'; the natural chain-rule decomposition from the endpoint (D_KL(path) = D_KL(q1||p1) + non-negative backward conditional KLs) is never written out. In Eqs. (53)-(55), O(ε) terms are kept inside logarithms with ratios of small quantities, and the O(ε^2) claim for the d_H > 1 sum implicitly assumes bounded likelihood ratios that are not verified.

Section 5 ('Future Work: Chains of Discrete Flows') is explicitly untested speculation, including its own list of open questions; the training-stability discussion similarly consists of unvalidated proposals ('could... for example would be using a moving average'). These belong in a discussion, not as contributions.

No discussion of limitations or failure modes of the proposed objectives (e.g., that minimizing expected outflow may conflict with model quality, that minibatch OT bias grows with batch-size reduction, that the bound in Eq. (24) may be loose when learned velocities are near zero, making w log(w/v) terms unstable).

Presentation issues: mixed integral/sum notation over discrete spaces (Eqs. 11, 16), typos ('less ambitions', 'moves form 0 to 1', 'One such strategy could for example would be'), and no code or reproducibility material. With no experiments, there is nothing to reproduce beyond the theorems.

The practical significance of the Hamming-cost Kantorovich objective is questionable by the paper's own admission: for large vocabularies with independent source/target samples, positions rarely match exactly, so the paper itself notes 'we should not expect substantial improvements by optimizing the Kantorovich expression using minibatches'—undercutting the motivation for the primary contribution in the very section that introduces it.

strengths: The manuscript is clearly written, with a well-organized presentation of the discrete flow matching framework and a careful, mostly self-contained derivation style.

Theorem 3.1 (equivalence between a dynamic-style discrete objective and a Kantorovich formulation with cost given by a sum of token-similarity terms) and Corollaries 3.2-3.3 (Hamming distance and embedding L2 cost as special cases) are clean results, and the proofs in Appendix A appear correct and complete.

The perplexity upper bound (Theorem 4.1 / Eq. 24) addresses a genuine practical gap: unlike continuous flows, discrete flow models lack a change-of-variables density estimator, so a computable cross-entropy bound is a useful evaluation tool for the community.

The paper is honest that the 'chains of flows' idea is untested (Section 5 is explicitly labeled future work), and the discussion of training stability issues (embedding coupling feedback loop) shows awareness of practical pitfalls.
weaknesses: The paper contains no experiments whatsoever. Every methodological proposal (minibatch OT coupling for discrete flows, similarity-metric-weighted objectives, modified source distributions, perplexity bound estimation, flow chains) is presented only as theory or unvalidated conjecture. For a paper whose core motivation is empirical ('reduce jumps', 'better use of similarity', 'enable evaluation and comparison'), the complete absence of even a toy-dataset validation of the bound's tightness or of the coupling's effect on generation quality is a fundamental deficiency.

The central theoretical result is largely anticipated by existing work and, upon inspection, is nearly immediate: in flow matching with interpolants, the marginal path is entirely determined by the coupling π, so Theorem 3.1 mostly restates that the expected number of jumps under the convex interpolant path telescopes to the Hamming/similarity cost of the coupling. The novelty over Tong et al. (2023) (minibatch OT for continuous FM) and Gat et al. (2024) (discrete FM, including couplings) is limited to an algebraic identity rather than a new minimization principle. Notably, the dynamic objective is never actually minimized by any training procedure — the paper only swaps the coupling heuristic.

The claimed 'Benamou-Brenier for discrete distributions' framing is overstated: the kinetic-energy analogy (Eq. 17 vs. Eq. 15) is informal, the objective is not shown to be an entropy-regularized transport problem, and no variational equivalence at the level of velocities/couplings (as in true Benamou-Brenier) is established.

The perplexity bound is adopted almost directly from Opper & Sanguinetti (2007) via Lou et al. (2024); its tightness, bias under the learned network, or behavior in practice are never assessed, undermining the claim that it 'enables performance evaluation and comparison with other methods.'

Section 5 is a future-work section describing an unimplemented method ('Chains of Discrete Flows'), listed as a main contribution in the introduction. Presenting an untested proposal as a contribution, with open questions left unresolved, signals an immature submission.

The paper lacks a limitations discussion, reproducibility artifacts (no code, since there is nothing to run), and leaves practical feasibility of the bound unstated: computing Eq. (24) requires expectations over the full coupling and the learned velocity, whose cost and bias are unquantified.

Minor presentation issues further reduce polish: inconsistent notation (e.g., 'z1' vs. target distribution q, subscript/superscript inconsistencies in velocity expressions, Eq. 16 describing Hamming cost as if it were Eq. 16's L2 cost), and Section 2.2 leaving an incomplete sentence ('z1 is an easy reference distribution...').

strengths: The paper identifies two genuine gaps in discrete flow matching: the lack of a coupling/OT-based path-straightening mechanism (rectification does not transfer to stochastic discrete paths) and the lack of a likelihood/perplexity evaluation mechanism.

The equivalence between the similarity-weighted dynamic objective (Eq. 18) and the Kantorovich cost Σ_i s(x0^i, x1^i) (Theorem 3.1) is cleanly derived for convex interpolant conditional flows, and the corollaries are elegant: the discrete metric yields the Hamming distance, and embedding-L2 similarity recovers the continuous-case L2 cost.

The perplexity upper bound (Theorem 4.1, building on Opper & Sanguinetti's Markov-jump KL bound) is a useful community tool, since discrete flows lack an instantaneous change-of-variables formula; the derivation strategy is plausible and the end result (Eq. 24) is a computable bound under the standard flow matching parameterization.

The paper is generally well motivated and, to its credit, openly acknowledges weaknesses, e.g., that minibatch Kantorovich optimization should not help substantially when the source distribution is uninformative (mask-only source).
weaknesses: There are no experiments at all. Every practical claim — reducing state transitions, better use of source–target similarity, the proposed empirical-token and K-means source distributions, bound tightness, comparison of perplexity against other methods — is left unvalidated. For an ICML main-track paper whose abstract advertises 'performance evaluation and comparison with other methods', the complete absence of any empirical evidence is a decisive weakness.

The theoretical novelty is modest. Theorem 3.1 is essentially the discrete/categorical analogue of the known Benamou–Brenier ↔ Kantorovich equivalence for minibatch-OT flow matching (Tong et al., 2023), and the proof follows directly from the linear interpolant structure (the κ-integral telescopes to (κ1−κ0)). Theorem 4.1 adapts a known Markov-jump-process result (Opper & Sanguinetti, 2007) and is explicitly motivated by Lou et al. (2024); the paper does not clearly delineate how this bound differs from or improves upon existing ELBO-style likelihood bounds for discrete diffusion (Lou et al., 2024; Sahoo et al., 2024) or the standard flow matching ELBO.

The paper's own argument undercuts its headline motivation: for the most common source distributions (mask token or uniform), only a tiny proportion of positions match exactly, so 'we should not expect substantial improvements by optimizing the Kantorovich expression using minibatches.' The proposed fixes (empirical-token or K-means source distributions, embedding-based similarity, moving-average embedding stabilization) are stated but never tested.

The proof of Theorem 4.1 has loose error bookkeeping. Terms of order O(ε) and O(ε²) are handled per-state (Eqs. 53–57, 67–68), but the sums run over exponentially many states and K = ⌊1/ε⌋ time steps; it is not shown that the accumulated error terms vanish in the ε→0 limit, particularly for the third sum and the O(ε) inside the log ratio in Eq. 68. Additionally, no discussion is given of bound tightness in practice, e.g., when the learned velocity v_i is near zero while w_i > 0, the log(w/v) term diverges.
Section 5 (chains of discrete flows) is presented as a contribution but is purely speculative future work with acknowledged untested trade-offs, further diluting the substance of the submission.

Presentation has notable polish issues: undefined notation (z1 in §2.2), inconsistent dimension symbols (N vs. L; [d] vs. [V]), typos ('less ambitions', 'One such strategy could for example would be'), and Corollary numbering inconsistency (the text cites 'Corollary 1' while the contribution is labeled Corollary 3.2).

strengths: The paper addresses a genuine and timely gap: rectification/OT-based trajectory simplification does not carry over trivially to discrete flow matching (DFM) because discrete paths are stochastic. The weighted path-length dynamic objective (Eq. 11) and its Kantorovich counterpart (Theorem 3.1) are clean, general (arbitrary similarity s), and fully proved for the convex-interpolant class used in practice (Gat et al., 2024), with Hamming and L2-embedding costs recovered as corollaries.

The two computable upper bounds on DFM perplexity (Theorems 4.1-4.2, Propositions 4.3-4.4) extend KL/entropy-derivation techniques from Opper & Sanguinetti (2007), Lou et al. (2024) and Haxholli et al. (2025) to DFM, and the paper honestly situates them against the concurrent ELBO-based result of Shaul et al. (2025). They enable principled likelihood-based training (DFM-N) and cross-model comparison with SEDD and GPT-2 (Tables 2, 6), which is a real practical asset given DFM previously lacked likelihood evaluation.

The multi-mask flow (Section 3.2) is a clever construction: it preserves the time-independence of predictive probabilities of masked flows (proved in Proposition A.2) while making the source distribution non-degenerate so that minibatch OT becomes applicable. It empirically outperforms masked DFM in generative perplexity (Table 3) without entropy/diversity loss (Table 12).

Experiments are substantive and reproducible-friendly: GPT-2-scale training on OWT, both GPT-2-large and Llama 3.1-8B judges with standard deviations, entropy checks for diversity, transport-cost verification of the theory (Table 13), tightness analysis of the bounds (~11% gap in a toy setting, plus a theoretical tight case), OT overhead scaling analysis (Table 4), and ablations over solver and OT batch size. The 8-fold inference-step reduction (1024 to 128) for BoW-sourced flows is a meaningful practical result.
Limitations are discussed candidly (interacting OT/flow optimizations, embedding drift affecting couplings), and the paper includes a transparency statement on LLM usage.
weaknesses: The headline 'categorical Benamou-Brenier theorem' is weaker than the name suggests. As the authors concede in Remark 3.4, for convex interpolants the dynamic loss equals the static cost pointwise for every coupling, so the 'infimum over couplings is purely formal'; there is no velocity-field optimization, no geodesic/optimality characterization, and the result is essentially a direct computation of an expected jump cost under the interpolant (Appendix A.1). Given the concurrent Shaul et al. (2025), which derives a kinetic-energy OT objective and a similar likelihood bound for DFM classes, the incremental theoretical novelty is moderate and the presentation occasionally oversells it.

Empirical gains are modest and the evaluation is partly soft. Generative perplexity under LLM judges is an imperfect metric; DFM-MMLM improvements over masked DFM are consistent but small (e.g., 141.92 vs 143.48 at 1024 steps), and Table 7 shows OT actually worsens the bound on Lambada for DFM-B while improving other sets. The central quantitative claim (8-fold step reduction) applies only to BoW sources, which the authors themselves note are required for OT couplings to matter on large vocabularies - a fairly restrictive practical setting.

Bound estimation for OT-trained models is acknowledged to be heuristic (Appendix C.3, Table 7), since the minibatch OT coupling is implicit and inaccessible; this weakens the claim that the bounds serve as reliable evaluation for exactly the models OT is applied to. Tightness is only characterized in toy settings (~11% gap) and for a state-independent chain.

Scale and scope are limited: all main experiments are GPT-2-sized models at sequence length 128 (1024 only for the bound comparisons in Table 2), with no comparison to discrete-diffusion baselines trained with OT, and no evidence of scaling behavior of the DFM-N/OT combination at larger model sizes, despite claims that relative OT overhead decreases with scale.

Presentation issues: inconsistent model naming (DFM-MMLM vs DFM-MMLMLM), small numeric inconsistencies between Table 3 and Table 10 (e.g., DFM-B at 128 and 1024 steps: 192.75/185.12 vs 191.48/185.83), typos in Appendix C.4 ('show show resutls', 'Such resulrs'), and some typos in the equations/derivations (e.g., Eq. 107, 118), which reduce polish and slightly hamper verification of the dense proofs.

strengths: The paper is technically careful: the Kantorovich equivalence (Theorem 3.1) is proven in detail, the KL/entropy identities (Theorem 4.1, Propositions 4.3–4.4) extend known variational techniques to DFM with full derivations in the appendix, and the masked-source special case correctly recovers the MD4 bound, which is a useful consistency check.

The perplexity upper bounds are a genuinely useful practical contribution: they provide a computable likelihood-like metric for DFM models and enable direct comparison with autoregressive (GPT-2) and discrete diffusion (SEDD) baselines, with a reported bound-vs-truth gap of ~11% in tractable settings.

The empirical finding that minibatch OT reduces inference steps 8-fold (1024→128) at matched generative perplexity is practically relevant, and the computational overhead analysis (Tables 4, 13–17) is thorough, covering batch size, solver choice, sequence length, and embedding-dimension scaling.

The multimask source construction (DFM-MMLM) is a sensible design that preserves the time-independence property of masked flows (proven in Appendix A.6) while permitting nontrivial couplings, and it improves generative perplexity without the entropy drop seen in improperly sampled SEDD.
Experimental details (architecture, optimizer, schedules, seeds/deviations across judges) are reported at a level that supports reasonable reproducibility, and a limitations section is included.
weaknesses: Limited originality. The central theoretical results substantially overlap concurrent work the paper itself acknowledges: Shaul et al. (ICLR 2025) already derive a kinetic-energy OT objective for discrete flows and independently obtain a similar likelihood bound, and the perplexity bounds are direct extensions of Opper & Sanguinetti (2007) and Haxholli et al. (2025) to DFM. The remaining novelty — Theorem 3.1 — is an elementary computation (integrating convex-interpolant velocities against a similarity cost) for a narrow class of interpolants, and Remark 3.4 concedes that 'taking the infimum over all couplings is purely formal', weakening the 'Benamou-Brenier-type theorem' framing.

The empirical setting is restricted. The headline 8-fold step reduction is obtained only with a Bag-of-Words source distribution; for the practically dominant masked-source flows, the trivial coupling precludes OT (acknowledged in Section 3). Thus the main claim does not apply to the regime where masked DFM is actually strongest.

Evidence for the core claims is noisy and indirect. All quality assessments rely on GPT-2-large/Llama-judged generative perplexity rather than likelihood on held-out data (where the bound is admittedly only a heuristic approximation for OT-trained models, per Appendix C.3), human evaluation, or downstream tasks. The reported Pearson correlation of 0.96 between bound and generative perplexity conflates models from the same family and does not validate the bound's tightness in realistic settings.

Model scale and baselines are modest: GPT-2-small-sized models at sequence length 128 trained on OWT, compared mainly against SEDD and GPT-2. Given that concurrent masked diffusion work evaluates at 1.1B parameters, the claims of competitiveness and of the bounds' practical utility are under-supported at this scale.

Bound tightness is only established in a two-token toy setting; in realistic language-modeling settings it cannot be estimated, which undercuts the framing of the bounds as 'principled' model comparison metrics.

Presentation issues remain: several typos ('form' for 'from', 'resutls', '12,57' decimal errors), dense notation with heavy index bookkeeping, and no explicit statement of code availability, which further limits reproducibility of the exact training pipeline despite the hyperparameter details given.

strengths: The paper addresses a genuine gap: discrete flow matching lacks deterministic paths, so continuous-flow tools (rectification, change-of-variables) do not apply. The proposed remedies—jump-minimizing OT couplings and perplexity upper bounds—are well-motivated and directly relevant to current language-modeling research.

The theoretical development is careful and mostly self-contained. The extension of the Opper & Sanguinetti / Haxholli et al. KL machinery to DFM (Theorems 4.1–4.2, Propositions 4.3–4.4) is non-trivial, and the masked-source special case recovering MD4 (Appendix A.4) is a good consistency check showing the bounds unify existing results.

Experiments are reasonably thorough for the claimed scale: proof-of-concept jump-reduction studies, GPT-2-scale training on OpenWebText with multiple baselines (DFM-B/S/N/O, DFM-MMLM ± OT), both GPT-2-large and Llama judges, entropy/diversity checks, timing/scaling analysis of OT overhead, and ablations on OT solver and batch size. The 8-fold inference-step reduction claim is supported by Table 3.

The multimask source construction (DFM-MMLM) is a clever practical contribution that makes OT applicable to masked-flow-style models while preserving time-independent predictive probabilities (Proposition A.2).

Reproducibility is good: architecture, hyperparameters, training schedules, and hardware are specified in detail; algorithms for OT training and both bound evaluations are given; appendices contain full proofs and complete result tables including standard deviations. The honest discussion of the coupling-intractability issue for bound evaluation of OT-trained models (Appendix C.3) is commendable.
Limitations are candidly discussed (Section 7), including the interacting-optimization issue with embedding-based similarities, and an LLM usage statement is provided.
weaknesses: The central 'Benamou-Brenier-type theorem' is weaker than the framing suggests. Remark 3.4 concedes that the dynamic-static equality (Theorem 3.1) holds pointwise for each coupling, so taking an infimum over couplings is 'purely formal.' This is an algebraic identity for convex-interpolant flows rather than a variational characterization, and it applies only to the specific interpolant family—so calling it a categorical Benamou-Brenier theorem overstates the contribution somewhat.

The novelty of the perplexity bounds is diminished by concurrent work: the authors themselves note Shaul et al. (2025) independently obtained a similar bound via ELBO, and Proposition 4.4 is explicitly a DFM extension of Haxholli et al. (2025). The remaining originality rests on the DFM extension and the OT/jump-reduction angle.

The headline OT gains are demonstrated only for BoW source distributions, which are niche in practice; the standard masked source admits only trivial couplings, which motivates the multimask variant but leaves the practical reach of minibatch OT uncertain. The Shakespeare experiments show modest gains (~5–14% jump reduction) and the character-level case already shows the Hamming metric becoming ineffective.

Bound tightness is validated only in toy settings (3-token, length-2); in realistic settings the gap is unquantified, and the reported ~11% toy gap plus the lack of an accessible coupling for OT-trained models means the bounds used for model comparison (e.g., Table 6) are heuristic for the OT variants.

Evaluation relies primarily on generative perplexity judged by GPT-2-large/Llama, a noisy proxy; while entropy and standard deviations are reported, human evaluation or downstream task evaluation is absent. All experiments are at GPT-2 scale (124M), so scaling claims (e.g., that relative OT overhead decreases with model size) are extrapolation.

The writing in Sections 4.1–4.2 is dense and the notation heavy (r_qt, r_pt, forward/reverse velocities), which impedes readability of the paper's second main contribution, even with the detailed appendices.
